question: According to Eurostat data, millions of businesses permanently shup up shop in the EU each year, highlighting the need to support their sustainability and not just their establishment. At the same time, according to the EU Payment Observatory’s 2025 report, 52 % of European businesses experienced problems due to late payments in 2024 and the average time it took public bodies to settle their bills was 69.8 days.

Small and medium-sized businesses form the backbone of the Greek economy and employment in the country. Nevertheless, high operating costs, bureaucracy and limited access to finance make it difficult for them to function. Late payments for services provided deprive them of necessary liquidity, making it difficult for them to pay wages and cover their overheads, even for companies with growth prospects.
In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
How does it view the implementation of EU rules on late payments in Greece and what actions does it intend to take to ensure that businesses are paid on time, particularly by public bodies?
What specific steps will it take to ensure that Greek micro-enterprises have effective access to affordable working capital through European financial tools?
Does it intend to boost targeted actions to support enterprises in their first years of business, reducing administrative burdens and protecting jobs?
